newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan trade surplus surges, U.S. voices concern.
newsitem.headline: Japan trade surplus surges, U.S. voices concern.

text.p: Japan's surplus in its current account, the broadest measure of trade in goods and services, rose sharply in January -- the first increase in 17 months, the Finance Ministry said on Thursday.

The fresh data, which showed a surge in the surplus to 150.7 billion yen ($1.24 billion) in January from 32.6 billion yen ($269 million) a year earlier, prompted a quick expression of concern from a U.S. government official.
"If this indicates a trend upward, then it would be a matter of concern to us, as Deputy Treasury Secretary (Lawrence) Summers made clear," the official told Reuters in Tokyo.
"Clearly the reduction (in the current account surplus) has bottomed out, so there is concern that it might be headed back up," the official added.
Japan's surplus in merchandise trade alone, a narrower measure of trade, fell to 229.3 billion yen ($1.89 billion) from 271.3 billion yen ($2.24 billion) a year earlier.

The surge in the current account surplus confounded analysts' forecasts, which ranged from a big deficit in the current account to a modest increase in the surplus. In a Reuters poll, the average of economists' forecasts had been for a deficit of 31 billion yen ($256 million).
January figures are notoriously unpredictable as the length of the New Year holiday, including weekends, varies from year to year, affecting the number of business days.

The contentious current account surplus fell in December for the 16th consecutive month of year-on-year declines. But the pace of the drop has slowed due to the yen's fall since mid-1995, which has boosted exports while discouraging imports.
A Japanese Finance Ministry official said after the figures were released that the current account surplus was still falling, but added that the pace of the decline had slowed.

"There are two reasons the surplus is going up. One, because the yen has been so weak for the past year and a half and the other is that domestic demand is going to be very dull," said Richard Jerram, chief economist at ING Baring in Tokyo.

U.S. officials have begun warning Tokyo against exporting its way out of its current economic woes. Despite low interest rates, the economy has been struggling to gain momentum after a long slump and a tax rise in April may put an even bigger squeeze on the recovery.

In a speech last Friday and in a news conference here earlier this week, Summers urged Japan to make sure its economic recovery was led by domestic growth, and that its trade surplus did not bulge again.
Summers also said Japan might need to take extra steps to ensure those objectives were met, depending on "how economic events played out".

U.S. officials have become particularly worried that Tokyo's plans to reduce its budget deficit, including a rise in its sales tax in April, could undermine growth and hence lead to a resurgence of its current account and trade surpluses.

Japanese Finance Ministry officials, meanwhile, have said Tokyo would stick to its policy of ensuring a domestic demand-led recovery and insist that Washington need not fear that Japan's trade surplus was set to balloon after halving since 1994. ($1=121 yen)
